terms.definition: An account in Linux that allows someone or something to log into the system and access resources like files, commands, and processes. Contains a username, password, UID, home directory, default shell, and primary group.
terms.example: ec2-user is the default normal user account on Amazon Linux EC2 instances

terms.definition: The most powerful user account on any Linux system, also called the superuser. Has UID 0 and complete administrative privileges — can install software, manage all users, modify any file, and run any command.
terms.example: root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash — this entry in /etc/passwd shows the root account with UID 0

terms.definition: A human user account created by the system administrator. Has a UID of 1000 or above, limited privileges, and a home directory at /home/username.
terms.example: On Amazon Linux EC2, ec2-user is the default normal user with UID 1000

terms.definition: An account automatically created by Linux or software installations to run background services and processes. Also called a service account. Has a UID between 1 and 999, cannot be used for login.
terms.example: The sshd user (UID 74) runs the SSH daemon service in the background

terms.definition: A unique number assigned to every user account that Linux uses internally to identify the user. UID 0 = root, 1–999 = system users, 1000+ = normal users.
terms.example: id vikram shows: uid=1001(vikram) — the UID is 1001

terms.definition: A unique number assigned to every group in Linux. Stored in /etc/group and also shown in /etc/passwd as the user's primary group ID.
terms.example: groups=1001(vikram),1002(developers) — the GID for developers group is 1002

terms.definition: A personal folder allocated to each user account, typically at /home/username. This is where the user's files and configuration data are stored. Acts like a private apartment for the user.
terms.example: ec2-user's home directory is /home/ec2-user; root's home directory is /root

terms.definition: The command interpreter automatically launched when a user logs in. Interprets the commands typed by the user and communicates with the Linux kernel. Most commonly /bin/bash.
terms.example: A user entry ending in /bin/bash uses the Bash shell; /sbin/nologin means the account cannot log in

terms.definition: The single group that is automatically created for every user when their account is created, using the same name as the user. Files created by the user are associated with this group by default.
terms.example: When useradd vikram is run, a group called vikram is automatically created as his primary group

terms.definition: Additional groups beyond the primary group that a user can be added to. Used to grant access to shared resources. A user can belong to many secondary groups.
terms.example: Adding vikram to the developers group with usermod -aG developers vikram makes developers a secondary group

terms.definition: A special group on Amazon Linux, CentOS, and RHEL that grants members the ability to use sudo (run commands as root temporarily). Adding a user to wheel gives them admin capabilities.
terms.example: sudo usermod -aG wheel username — grants sudo access on Amazon Linux

terms.definition: A special group on Ubuntu and Debian that grants members the ability to use sudo. Functionally equivalent to the wheel group on RHEL-based distributions.
terms.example: sudo usermod -aG sudo username — grants sudo access on Ubuntu

terms.definition: A command that allows normal users to temporarily run a specific command with root privileges without switching to the root account. Short for 'superuser do'.
terms.example: sudo cat /etc/shadow — runs cat as root to read the shadow file that normal users cannot access

terms.definition: A system file that stores basic information about every user account: username, UID, GID, home directory, and default shell. Readable by all users. Password field shows 'x' (actual passwords are in /etc/shadow).
terms.example: cat /etc/passwd — displays all user accounts and their basic information

terms.definition: A highly restricted system file that stores encrypted (hashed) passwords for all user accounts. Only readable by root. Stores the actual password hashes, not plaintext.
terms.example: sudo cat /etc/shadow — must use sudo because this file is only accessible by root

terms.definition: A system file that stores information about all groups: group name, GID, and list of member users. Used by Linux to resolve group memberships and apply group permissions.
terms.example: cat /etc/group shows: developers:x:1002:vikram,priya — group name, GID, and members

terms.definition: The Linux command to create a new user account. Automatically creates the account, a primary group, and a home directory. Requires root/sudo.
terms.example: sudo useradd vikram — creates the vikram user account

terms.definition: The Linux command to modify an existing user account. Can change groups, home directory, shell, lock/unlock the account. Requires root/sudo.
terms.example: sudo usermod -aG developers vikram — adds vikram to the developers group

terms.definition: The Linux command to delete a user account. The -r flag also removes the user's home directory. Requires root/sudo.
terms.example: sudo userdel -r vikram — deletes vikram's account and /home/vikram directory

terms.definition: A protocol for securely connecting to a remote Linux server over a network. Uses port 22. AWS EC2 instances use SSH with key pair authentication by default.
terms.example: ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@13.233.45.67 — connects to an EC2 instance using SSH

terms.definition: A pair of cryptographic keys used for SSH authentication: a private key (kept on your laptop) and a public key (stored in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server). More secure than passwords.
terms.example: The .pem file downloaded when creating an EC2 key pair is the private key

terms.definition: A file located at ~/.ssh/authorized_keys inside a user's home directory that stores the public SSH keys allowed to connect to that account. SSH authentication checks this file.
terms.example: When you create an EC2 instance with a key pair, AWS stores your public key in /home/ec2-user/.ssh/authorized_keys
